records.name: Antibody-guided effector mechanisms (ADCC, ADCP, CDC)
records.tldr: An antibody that coats a cell can lead to its removal in three different ways: immune cells that kill it, cells that swallow it, or blood proteins that damage its membrane. Seeing the coat does not show which of these happened.
records.summary:
Opsonisation means coating a target with molecules that help immune clearance. The antibody's Fc region can then connect that coat to effector cells or to complement, and three mechanisms name different downstream jobs. In antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) an effector cell, with the natural killer cell as the familiar example, triggers damage or death in a coated target, typically through an Fc gamma receptor such as CD16 engaging target-bound IgG. In antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP) a phagocyte such as a macrophage engulfs the coated target. In complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC) the complement protein C1q recognises a suitable arrangement of Fc regions and the cascade can end in membrane attack complexes. ADCC is not an exclusive cell-identity label: other immune populations can contribute antibody-dependent cytotoxicity.

The three routes can overlap and no universal ranking exists. Isotype and Fc design, target density, inhibitory signals and the availability of effectors or complement shape the result. Evidence differs in kind. Clynes et al. (2000) used mouse tumour models, including xenografts treated with the humanised antibodies trastuzumab and rituximab, and found that engagement of Fc gamma receptors on effector cells was a dominant component of in vivo antibody activity, with the inhibitory receptor FcgammaRIIB regulating it. Gül et al. (2014) imaged mice directly: liver macrophages (Kupffer cells) sampled circulating tumour cells without eliminating them, whereas antitumour antibody treatment produced rapid phagocytosis that depended on the Fc receptors FcgammaRI and FcgammaRIV. Diebolder et al. (2014) showed in cell and biochemical systems that ordered IgG hexamers assembled on the target surface recruit and activate C1, and that this could be manipulated to block or enhance complement killing across all four human IgG subclasses. None of these is a human treatment-benefit result.

What each step shows is separate. Fc-receptor binding is not completed ADCC or ADCP. A phagocyte touching a target, or sampling a fragment, is not internalisation of a whole viable cell. Complement deposition (coating) is an earlier step than a membrane pore, and a pore is a different observation from measured lysis. Assays therefore name their output: target death for ADCC, the fraction of phagocytes with verified internalised targets for ADCP, membrane damage with active complement for CDC (heat-inactivated or depleted complement tests complement dependence). They use viable targets, defined antibody concentrations, no-antibody and target-negative controls, and report exposure time and effector-to-target ratio. Binding or reporter activation alone is an earlier readout, and stronger activity in a dish does not establish clinical benefit or healthy-tissue safety.

records.name: Antibody structure (Fab, Fc and hinge)
records.tldr: An antibody has tips that find a target and a stem that can connect to other parts of the immune system. Two antibodies can reach the same target and do different jobs.
records.summary:
A typical immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibody has two heavy and two light chains held together by molecular interactions and disulfide bonds. At each arm tip, variable regions from a heavy and a light chain together form a binding site; its sequence and three-dimensional shape influence what it recognises. Fab (fragment antigen-binding) names an arm containing the binding site and its associated constant domains, so it is not simply another word for the variable region. Fc (fragment crystallizable, a name that comes from an experimental property) names the remaining stem, built from CH2 and CH3 domains of both heavy chains in the familiar IgG description. Hinge flexibility changes how the arms are arranged. A drawn Y is a simplification: some natural and engineered formats omit familiar parts.

Fc can interact with immune-cell receptors and with complement, but compatible effectors, target arrangement and other conditions decide whether killing, engulfment or complement damage follows, so Fc is not an automatic kill command. Binding and effector contributions are separate and the finished molecule needs testing. Nimmerjahn and Ravetch (2005) showed in mouse experiments that IgG subclasses differ in the ratio of their binding to activating and inhibitory Fc receptors, which predicted in vivo activity; that is not a universal ranking of human antibody performance. An isotype is a heavy-chain class (see the isotypes and Fc silencing record). Structure alone does not identify the producing cell or establish what the antibody recognises.

The epitope is the molecular feature recognised and can be a folded protein surface or another accessible feature, not necessarily a short fragment displayed by HLA. Binding is measured against a defined antigen preparation and antibody concentration, sometimes in nanomoles per litre, and it matters whether the test used purified protein or intact cells, because folding, accessibility and multiple binding sites change the result. A concentration or fluorescence signal alone is not an affinity. Fc-receptor and complement interactions are tested separately from target binding, and neither binding nor a laboratory effector result establishes clinical benefit or safety. A blocking antibody, an antibody-drug conjugate and a bispecific format can share a target and still act differently.

records.name: B cells, plasmablasts and plasma cells
records.tldr: B cells recognise a target and can develop into cells that make large amounts of antibody. A cell's presence tells you little about what its antibody recognises or whether it helps against a cancer.
records.summary:
A developing B cell assembles an antigen-receptor sequence by V(D)J recombination. Its B-cell receptor contains membrane-bound immunoglobulin and recognises an accessible molecular feature, unlike a conventional T-cell receptor, which recognises peptide held by HLA. Recognition and activation are separate steps. For many protein antigens B cells receive help from suitable CD4 T cells and can internalise recognised material and present fragments to those helpers, while other antigen contexts support responses with less direct T-cell help.

An activated response can leave memory B cells and antibody-secreting cells. A plasmablast is an early antibody-secreting stage that can still divide; plasma cells are further specialised for secretion, some short-lived and some persisting in supportive tissue niches. Memory B cells are not simply plasma cells waiting to secrete. Shapiro-Shelef et al. (2003) deleted the gene for Blimp-1 (prdm1) in mouse B cells: B-cell development and the number of antigen-responding B cells looked normal, yet serum immunoglobulin, short-lived plasma cells, post-germinal-centre plasma cells and memory-response plasma cells were virtually absent, so responding to antigen was not enough for normal secretion. This is a mechanistic mouse experiment, not a human tumour biomarker rule. Some responses pass through germinal centres, where B-cell variants undergo selection; class switching changes antibody class and sequence changes with selection can alter binding quality, which are different processes.

In tumour samples, B cells can present material, supply signals and make antibody, and plasma cells can contribute a large share of immunoglobulin RNA, so a high immunoglobulin signal does not show that cancer cells made it. Neither more B cells nor more antibody is a universal benefit rule; B cells may sit in tertiary lymphoid structures. Flow cytometry and spatial staining distinguish populations by marker combinations that change with differentiation, so a panel for ordinary B cells can miss plasma cells; keep the phenotype definition and the denominator. RNA can show an antibody-production programme or receptor sequence and serum assays measure concentration and class, but what an antibody recognises needs antigen-specific binding and functional tests. Plasma cells are cells, not blood plasma, which is the fluid part of blood.

records.name: Antibody isotypes and Fc silencing
records.tldr: An antibody's class and the design of its stem change how it connects to immune cells and complement. Switching off one connection does not switch off all of them, and does not make the finished drug harmless.
records.summary:
An isotype is a heavy-chain class: IgM, IgD, IgG, IgA or IgE, and human IgG also has the subclasses IgG1, IgG2, IgG3 and IgG4. The classes differ in architecture, distribution and potential effector interactions. Vidarsson et al. (2014) review how the four IgG subclasses differ in their hinges and upper CH2 domains, which bind Fc gamma receptors and C1q, giving different effector functions, while the Fc also carries a binding site for the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) that extends half-life. A B-cell lineage can undergo class switching, changing the constant region while keeping the rearranged variable-region sequence; this differs from the mutations that change affinity during a response, and neither the class nor a switch says what antigen an antibody recognises. Subclass, Fc sugars, target geometry and the available cells all affect interactions, so IgG1 and IgG4 are not interchangeable but neither name fully predicts behaviour. As a real example, pembrolizumab is a humanised IgG4 kappa antibody (FDA label, section 11); its intended job is to block the PD-1 receptor, not to recruit killer cells to the T cells it binds.

Fc silencing uses design changes to reduce selected receptor or complement interactions. Lo et al. (2017) found that the commonly used N297G and D265A/N297G variants, effective at attenuating effector function in primates, retained potent complement activation in mice and created safety liabilities in murine studies, whereas an L234A, L235A, P329G (LALA-PG) variant eliminated complement binding and attenuated effector activity in that setting. That supports engineering a particular interaction in a particular species; it does not prove universal human safety or silence in every assay. IgG4 is not a synonym for a fully silent Fc.

FcRn has a separate role in IgG transport and recycling, so reduced Fc gamma receptor recruitment does not by itself establish reduced FcRn binding or a shorter half-life. Compare matched molecules with the same binding regions and measure target binding, Fc gamma receptor and C1q binding, and killing, engulfment or complement damage separately, stating species, receptor variants, concentrations and effector cells; FcRn binding and exposure are further questions. An antibody meant to remove a target-bearing cell may benefit from effector recruitment, whereas one meant to block an immune receptor may need to avoid removing useful receptor-bearing cells, and a silenced Fc does not prevent target binding, payload toxicity or every source of inflammation.

records.name: Antigen-processing machinery (APM)
records.tldr: Cells cut up proteins, move some fragments to a loading site and place them on display molecules that T cells can inspect. Having a protein inside a cell does not guarantee its fragment is shown.
records.summary:
Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

Evidence layers differ. DNA sequence and copy number show gene retention or alteration but not expression or function; RNA shows sampled gene activity but not protein, assembly or display; protein staining or flow cytometry detects protein but not which peptide is shown; HLA-associated peptide recovery shows a peptide was recovered with HLA in that preparation but not its cell of origin or recognition; controlled T-cell recognition shows function against tested targets. Peptide loading can bypass processing, so rescue by supplied peptide supports a bottleneck under those conditions only. Binding prediction is not presentation, and CD4 help is not proof of CD8 tumour recognition.

records.name: HLA allele names and typing reports
records.tldr: HLA typing reads the inherited versions of the genes that display protein fragments. The name tells you how precisely the version is known, not whether a tumour still shows a given fragment.
records.summary:
In an allele name such as HLA-A*02:01:01:01 the fields carry distinct meanings (official HLA nomenclature). HLA-A is the gene; 02 is the allele group, which often corresponds to a serological antigen; the second field (01) distinguishes protein sequences within the group, since alleles differing there differ in at least one amino-acid-changing substitution; the third field distinguishes synonymous coding differences; the fourth distinguishes differences outside the coding region. An optional suffix gives expression status: N for a null allele, and L, S, C, A or Q for alternatively expressed alleles, L meaning significantly reduced surface expression. A name without a suffix is not a measurement of how much HLA a cancer cell expresses. A shared first field does not establish identical proteins, and a report stating only A*02 at group resolution cannot be silently completed as A*02:01.

People generally inherit one copy of each HLA gene from each parent, so a report lists two alleles per locus, which can be the same name. Class I and class II typing describe different display molecules. Typing identifies inheritance; it does not show tumour retention or expression, peptide display or receptor recognition, and a negative display assay does not by itself show the typing was wrong. Loss of an allele in the tumour, or changes in antigen-processing machinery, can interrupt the chain after an accurate typing result. A trial may name an allele and an accepted method; eligibility belongs to the study team and neither a similar name nor correct typing shows targetability.

Laboratory typing starts from an accepted specimen and extracted DNA, tests sequence patterns with primers or probes or reads selected regions by Sanger or next-generation sequencing, optionally after PCR amplification, and compares the result with a reference database (IPD-IMGT/HLA). Hosomichi et al. (2013) describe phase-defined sequencing of six HLA genes by long-range PCR and multiplex sequencing: phasing connects differences on the same inherited copy, and unresolved phase or a missing distinguishing region can leave alternative allele pairs despite good base quality. More reads of the same regions cannot settle such an ambiguity; the distinguishing information must be added, and both alternatives should be kept until it is. Software can infer class I HLA from genome, exome or RNA sequencing: Szolek et al. (2014) reported OptiType's overall accuracy of 97 per cent on their benchmark of RNA, exome and whole-genome data. Capture, coverage and expression affect such inference, and an inference is not automatically a laboratory result accepted for clinical use. Reports should be read with resolution, ambiguity notes, coverage, database version and validation.

The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 of them class I and 14,835 class II, so exact allele names matter.

Existing record hla-a-02-01 covers HLA-A*02:01 as an eligibility marker for TCR therapies; this record covers how names and reports are read.

records.name: HLA (human leukocyte antigen) and MHC
records.tldr: HLA molecules sit on cells and hold up small pieces of the cell's proteins for T cells to inspect. A T cell reads the fragment together with the particular HLA version holding it.
records.summary:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

records.name: Tumour-associated antigen (TAA)
records.tldr: A tumour-associated antigen is a target that is common in a tumour but can also be present in healthy tissue. A treatment aimed at it can affect both, and can also react with a different, look-alike target.
records.summary:
Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. A published example of the second is an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor directed at HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3: in a clinical study the first two treated patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days, no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and the T cells recognised an unrelated peptide from the striated-muscle protein titin (Linette et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013, who describe the preclinical analysis as having found no off-target concern). That illustrates the hazard for one engineered receptor and is not a toxicity rate for tumour-associated targets. Immune tolerance also shapes the available response to self antigens, and a stronger receptor does not remove the need to test healthy tissues and alternative targets.

A shared antigen can support a treatment intended for more than one person's cancer, with a trade-off between tumour coverage and healthy-tissue exposure; expression prevalence in a cohort is not a safe recognition threshold for a product. For vaccine-elicited peptide-specific T cells, a shared antigen offers another candidate when credible private targets are few, which is a coverage hypothesis, not demonstrated benefit. A peptide from a shared antigen and one from a neoantigen may depend on the same HLA allele, so changing the antigen does not restore a missing display route: Tran et al. (2016) documented escape after loss of the restricting HLA allele in one colorectal cancer patient. Antibodies and CARs have different recognition requirements, and epitope spreading is a separate widening of recognition that adding a shared antigen does not guarantee.

records.name: Antigen
records.tldr: An antigen is a molecular target an immune receptor can recognise. Recognition alone does not establish immune activation or safe tumour targeting.
records.summary: Most cancer antigens are ordinary human proteins that a tumour makes in unusual amounts (HER2, TROP2, CD19, PSMA), so drugs targeting them also touch normal cells that carry a little; truly tumour-specific antigens arise from mutations (neoantigens) or from viral proteins. A good drug antigen is abundant on tumour cells, scarce on essential normal tissue, and stable over time. Tumours escape by losing the antigen, which is how CD19-negative relapse defeats CAR-T, and by hiding the pieces of antigen they would normally display to T cells. Recognition differs from immunogenicity, the ability to elicit an immune response in a particular setting. An antibody can recognise an accessible part of a molecule directly, whereas a conventional peptide-directed T-cell receptor recognises a processed peptide together with a particular HLA molecule, so a surface-expression result cannot by itself establish peptide-HLA display. A self molecule can be an antigen, and tumour-associated is not the same as tumour-specific.

records.name: Epitope
records.tldr: An epitope is the molecular feature an immune receptor recognises. Antibodies and T-cell receptors can recognise different surfaces from the same source protein.
records.summary: An epitope is a molecular feature recognised by an immune receptor; its definition depends on the receptor and the tested molecular preparation. Trastuzumab and pertuzumab both bind HER2 but at different epitopes, which is why they can be given together, and zanidatamab is a single antibody built to grab both spots at once. For T cells, the epitope is a short peptide fragment held in an HLA molecule on the cell surface; an alteration that changes recognition can permit escape, but its effects on processing, display and other cell functions need their own evidence. The epitope an antibody recognises can be a continuous stretch of sequence or a surface formed by folding, so distant parts of the chain can meet; accessibility matters, and binding to an isolated protein does not show the same site is reachable on an intact cell. For a conventional T-cell receptor the target is the peptide together with the restricting HLA molecule, and the same peptide on another HLA molecule is a different recognition surface.

records.name: Antibody
records.tldr: A typical IgG antibody has antigen-binding arms and a stem that can interact with other parts of the immune system. Binding alone does not specify its function.
records.summary: A typical IgG has two antigen-binding arms; receptor binding and cross-reactivity depend on the particular molecule and test system, while its stem (the Fc region) can recruit immune cells and complement or extend the antibody's life in the blood. Therapeutic antibodies block growth receptors (trastuzumab on HER2, cetuximab on EGFR), release the brakes on T cells (pembrolizumab on PD-1), flag cancer cells for immune killing (rituximab on CD20), or serve as the targeting vehicle of ADCs and radioimmunotherapy. Bispecific formats have two binding specificities. Some are designed to bring a T cell and a target cell together; their structures and functions vary. Fab, the arm with the binding site, and Fc, the stem, are separate parts: binding does not guarantee killing, and Fc effector contacts need compatible effector cells or complement. Antibodies that bind the same target can act differently: a blocking antibody, an antibody-drug conjugate and a bispecific format can share a target and still differ in what follows.

records.name: B cell
records.tldr: B cells can develop into antibody-secreting cells or memory cells. Their presence does not identify what an antibody recognises or whether it helps against cancer.
records.summary: Each B cell makes one antibody; when it meets its antigen it multiplies and matures into plasma cells that pump out that antibody in bulk, which is the response the hybridoma technique captured to make monoclonal antibodies. B cells carry surface markers (CD19, CD20, CD22) throughout their lives and plasma cells carry BCMA, and these markers make B-cell cancers (most lymphomas, CLL, ALL, myeloma) the most successful targets of rituximab, CAR-T and bispecific antibodies; since normal B cells are also wiped out, patients need antibody replacement and are prone to infection. B cells inside solid tumours, organised into structures resembling lymph nodes, are associated with better responses to immunotherapy. Plasma cells are the antibody-secreting end of the lineage, plasmablasts an earlier dividing stage and memory B cells a separate lasting trace of a response; a high immunoglobulin RNA signal in a tumour sample can come from plasma cells and does not show that cancer cells made it.

records.name: ADCC (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity)
records.tldr: In ADCC, immune effector cells attack an antibody-coated target. NK cells are a familiar example; coating alone does not show completed killing.
records.summary: ADCC, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, is the process in which an antibody flags a cell and NK cells recognise the flag and kill it. In the familiar NK-cell route, the antibody Fc region interacts with FcγRIIIa (CD16). Changes to Fc sequence or glycans can alter receptor interactions; the resulting activity needs measurement in a defined system. ADCC contributes to the activity of trastuzumab, rituximab and cetuximab, and the mechanism belongs to the Monoclonal antibodies technology entry. Drug records that cite it include Margetuximab, Zolbetuximab, Obinutuzumab, Rituximab, Tafasitamab, Daratumumab, Mogamulizumab, Elotuzumab and Dinutuximab (ch14.18) / dinutuximab beta, and it is referenced by the Gastric & gastro-oesophageal junction cancer and Neuroblastoma (paediatric) entries. NK cells are the familiar example, not the only one: other immune cells can contribute antibody-dependent cytotoxicity, and phagocytes can instead engulf a coated cell (ADCP) or complement can damage its membrane (CDC). Receptor binding or contact does not show completed killing.

records.tldr: Fc engineering changes selected antibody interactions with immune cells, complement or recycling receptors. Each interaction needs its own measurement.
records.summary: Fc engineering means tweaking the antibody's tail, the Fc region, so that it recruits immune cells more strongly, or not at all. Fc sequence and glycan changes can alter effector recruitment. Fc-silencing variants reduce selected interactions in a defined system; an IgG4 backbone or an engineering label alone does not establish complete silence or human safety. FcRn-mediated recycling is a separate property. The term is linked to the Monoclonal antibodies and Bispecific antibodies technologies and to the terms Antibody, NK cell and Half-life. records.name: Dendritic-cell cross-presentation (cDC1)
records.tldr: Cross-presentation displays externally acquired protein fragments on class I HLA. Initial activation of a naive T cell is a further step called cross-priming.
records.summary:
Most cells display on MHC class I only peptides from proteins they make themselves, so a CD8 T cell is normally primed by an infected or transformed cell's own antigen. Cross-presentation is the route by which certain dendritic cells take up exogenous antigen (from dead cells or debris), move it from the phagosome into the cytosolic processing pathway and load it onto MHC class I, priming CD8 T cells against antigens they did not synthesise. The subset specialised for this is the type 1 conventional dendritic cell (cDC1): CD8alpha+ and CD103+ in mice, CD141 (BDCA-3)+ in humans, dependent on FLT3 ligand and the transcription factor BATF3 for development, internalising necrotic-cell material through CLEC9A (DNGR-1), a receptor for polymerised actin, and expressing the chemokine receptor XCR1, which favours contact with CD8 T cells (Alfaro et al., 2013).

The in vivo proof came from Batf3-deficient mice (Hildner et al., Science 2008): they lacked CD8alpha+ dendritic cells, their dendritic cells were defective in cross-presentation, and they failed to reject highly immunogenic syngeneic tumours. In mouse melanoma, CD103+ dendritic cells were the only antigen-presenting cells carrying intact antigen to lymph nodes and priming tumour-specific CD8 T cells, and they were required for PD-L1 blockade to work; expanding them with FLT3 ligand and activating them with intratumoral poly I:C improved responses to PD-L1 and BRAF inhibition (Salmon et al., Immunity 2016). This is why a scarcity of cDC1 in a tumour is read as one cause of a cold, checkpoint-resistant tumour, and why vaccine designs target antigen to cDC1 receptors such as CLEC9A, or expand and activate these cells, rather than relying on bulk monocyte-derived dendritic cells.

Cross-presentation names a display process, whereas cross-priming names the activation of naive CD8 T cells through it, which needs supporting signals and its own readout. Direct presentation remains possible: a dendritic cell that receives vaccine messenger RNA and makes the protein itself presents it directly. A cell can also acquire already assembled peptide-HLA complexes from another cell (cross-dressing), which does not show processing by the recipient (Wakim and Bevan, Nature 2011, PMID 21455179, mouse viral infection). External antigen on class II is not cross-presentation.

records.name: Complement in cancer
records.tldr: Complement proteins can coat targets, recruit inflammation and sometimes damage membranes. Complement deposition and completed target killing are different findings.
records.summary: Three routes converge on C3 convertase: classical (C1q binding IgG1/IgG3 Fc clusters, the basis of complement-dependent cytotoxicity by rituximab, obinutuzumab less so, daratumumab), lectin, and alternative (spontaneous C3 tick-over). C3b opsonises for phagocytosis via CR3; C5 convertase releases C5a and assembles the membrane attack complex (C5b-9). Tumours over-express membrane regulators CD46, CD55 (DAF) and CD59 (protectin) and secrete factor H, limiting CDC; CD20 shaving and antigen loss add to rituximab resistance. Conversely, intratumoural complement activation is often pro-tumour: C5a-C5aR1 and C3a-C3aR recruit and activate MDSCs and neutrophils, suppress CD8 T cells, and promote angiogenesis; C1q from macrophages supports invasion. Blocking C5aR1 (avdoralimab) with anti-PD-1 was tested; complement is also a mediator of infusion reactions and of CAR-T-associated inflammation. Fc engineering (afucosylation for ADCC versus hexamerisation for CDC) tunes which effector dominates. Complement deposition on a coated cell is an earlier step than a membrane pore, and a pore is a different observation from measured lysis, so deposition alone does not demonstrate completed CDC; heat-inactivated or depleted complement tests complement dependence.

records.name: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS)
records.tldr: Organised immune-cell clusters can form within or beside tumours. Their architecture and association with treatment outcomes depend on the study and assay.
records.summary:
Sautès-Fridman and colleagues review tertiary lymphoid structures as organised aggregates of B cells, T cells and dendritic cells that develop in chronically inflamed tissues including tumours, where they are generally associated with longer survival and response to checkpoint inhibitors. Because they are visible on H&E and spatial assays, they are a known-biology probe: a slide or spatial model that recovers TLS is learning something real. No medicine in OnCo is designed to build them. Two linked trials use them directly: a phase 3 trial in triple-negative breast cancer enrols only patients whose residual tumour contains them, and a pancreatic cancer vaccine trial counts how many patients form them as a primary outcome. In the retrospective immune checkpoint cohorts of Vanhersecke et al. (Nature Cancer 2021, PMID 35118423) a structure was called mature when at least one CD23-positive cell with dendritic morphology was found within it, and mature structures were associated with better response rate, progression-free survival and overall survival independently of PD-L1 status and CD8 density; a CD23-positive cell elsewhere in tissue does not establish that architecture. Any TLS were seen in 105 of 328 discovery-cohort cases (32 per cent), 84 of them mature. That is an association in treated cohorts, so it does not by itself show extra benefit from the treatment, and no universal abundance or maturity rule selects a therapy. Aggregate, B-cell follicle and germinal centre are different architectural levels, and an RNA signature alone cannot show a germinal centre. Report density with its area and the criteria used (structures per mm2; two organised structures in 4 mm2 is 0.5 per mm2), because thresholds are method- and study-specific, and small sections or disrupted architecture limit the reading.

Tertiary names where these structures form: ectopic lymphoid organisation in non-lymphoid tissue, including inflamed tissues and tumours. It does not name a cancer stage or establish a particular maturation level.

In untreated invasive breast-tumour specimens, Gu-Trantien and colleagues linked CXCL13-producing follicular helper T cells in TLS germinal centres and an eight-gene signature to group outcomes, including survival or preoperative chemotherapy response. In metastatic melanoma samples, Cabrita and colleagues associated co-occurring CD8-positive T cells and CD20-positive B cells with survival, and a derived TLS signature predicted outcomes in checkpoint-blockade cohorts. Each result retains its specimens, methods and setting; these associations do not establish that inducing a TLS will benefit a particular patient.

records.name: HLA-A*02:01 (HLA typing for TCR therapies)
records.tldr: HLA-A*02:01 is a specific allele used as an eligibility marker for some T-cell receptor therapies. Typing alone does not establish eligibility, target display or benefit.
records.summary: HLA typing by sequencing (the SeCore CDx HLA Sequencing System is the FDA-listed companion diagnostic for both drugs) reports the patient's HLA-A alleles. Tebentafusp (Kimmtrak) is labelled for HLA-A*02:01-positive adults with unresectable or metastatic uveal melanoma; afamitresgene autoleucel (Tecelra) for synovial sarcoma in patients who are HLA-A*02:01P, -A*02:02P, -A*02:03P or -A*02:06P positive and whose tumour expresses MAGE-A4 by the MAGE-A4 IHC 1F9 pharmDx, with HLA-A*02:05P as an exclusion allele. A typing report is read with its resolution: a group-level result such as HLA-A*02 cannot be completed as A*02:01, because the group holds different protein variants, and typing of inherited DNA does not show whether the tumour still expresses the allele or displays the target peptide.

records.tldr: B2M supplies a light-chain protein used by class I HLA and several related complexes. A variant or RNA result alone does not establish loss of these functions.

records.biology: Receptor for the Fc region of complexed or aggregated immunoglobulins gamma. Low affinity receptor. Involved in a variety of effector and regulatory functions such as phagocytosis of immune complexes and modulation of antibody production by B-cells. Binding to this receptor results in down-modulation of previous state of cell activation triggered via antigen receptors on B-cells (BCR), T-cells (TCR) or via another Fc receptor. Isoform IIB1 fails to mediate endocytosis or phagocytosis. Isoform IIB2 does not trigger phagocytosis. Location: Cell membrane (UniProt). Locus 1q23.3 (HGNC).
